title: Unit nine, mile marker one-oh-four
distinction_statement: The weak version gives both speakers the same careful middle register; the strong version identifies each of them by sentence length, idiom and tactic.
intention: A reader should hear two different people on one radio channel without the text labelling either of them.

change.description: Paragraph 2 replaces an identical-register exchange with a dispatcher speaking in logs and mile markers and a driver speaking in digressions and promises.

before.label: distinct_voices
before.text:
At ten past two the depot office smelled of diesel and instant coffee. Marla had the radio handset in one hand and a pen in the other, and the board above her showed eleven trucks, two of them stopped.

— Unit nine, you’re showing stopped at the weighbridge. Everything all right behind you?
— Yeah, yeah. I got a flat on the trailer and the boy here says he’s got no jack, so I’m waiting on the Lord and a fella from Sudbury. Listen, Marla, my wife’s sister is in the hospital in Barrie and I promised her I’d—
— I can’t hear promises. I hear mile markers. Where are you?
— Mile marker one-oh-four, and don’t you write that down like it’s my fault.
— One-oh-four. Logged.

She put the handset down, wrote 104 in the column and drew a small circle around it, the way she marked a delay that was nobody’s fault.

after.label: interchangeable_voices
after.text:
At ten past two the depot office smelled of diesel and instant coffee. Marla had the radio handset in one hand and a pen in the other, and the board above her showed eleven trucks, two of them stopped.

— I think it would be good if we checked the situation, because the situation is unpleasant.
— Yes, I think it would be good if we checked the situation, since the situation is unpleasant.
— Then let us look for an acceptable solution for both of us.
— I agree, let us look for an acceptable solution for both of us.

She put the handset down, wrote 104 in the column and drew a small circle around it, the way she marked a delay that was nobody’s fault.

expected_evidence.quote: — Yes, I think it would be good if we checked the situation, since the situation is unpleasant.
expected_evidence.expectation: quoted as an answer that repeats the other speaker almost word for word

expected_evidence.quote: I can’t hear promises. I hear mile markers.
expected_evidence.expectation: quoted as syntax and idiom that belong to one speaker only

acceptable_alternative_readings: Uniform, careful speech can be realistic on a recorded channel; the pair judges the written page, not radio protocol.
The driver’s digression can be read as unprofessional rather than as a distinct voice.
